summary: Describes an envelope that binds a file to one or more time-stamp tokens obtained for it, as defined in RFC 3161 or its successors. The file does not need to be cryptographically protected, and other kinds of temporal evidence are allowed too.

plainLanguage.summary: A date stamp proves when a paper existed. This note defines a wrapper that attaches such proofs of time to a file so they travel together.

questions: how to bind a file with a timestamp token
what is the time-stamp envelope syntax
how to bind a document to a time-stamp token
how to extend the validity of a time-stamp
subtitle: A CMS-based envelope that keeps a file and its time-stamp tokens together in one object.

tldr.problem: A time-stamp proves a document existed before a certain moment, but there is no standard way to keep the document and its time-stamps together. People use separate files or ad hoc envelopes, which hurts interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5544 defines a new CMS content type, timestamped-data, whose TimeStampedData structure holds the file (or a URI to it), optional metadata and a chain of RFC 3161 time-stamp tokens.
tldr.outcome: The format is Informational and not a candidate for any Internet Standard. The IESG note points readers to the standards-track Evidence Record Syntax (RFC 4998) as an alternative. RFC 5955 later updated it.

today: RFC 5544 is Informational and was updated by RFC 5955; it has not been obsoleted. It is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard, and the IESG note directs readers to also review RFC 4998.

sections.title: Why Bind a Document to Its Time-Stamps
sections.content:
Time-stamping is the standard technique for proving that a document existed before a certain point in time. Its value does not depend on digital signatures: it can be useful to time-stamp a document that is not signed, and sometimes mandatory to time-stamp a signed document in its entirety.

When a time-stamp relates to a signature, RFC 3161 already lets one or more TimeStampTokens ride inside a SignerInfo as unsigned attributes. For a time-stamped document as a whole there was no standard way to keep the pieces together. Typical workarounds were separate files, where the user tracks which time-stamp belongs to which document, or ad hoc solutions such as a ZIP archive or a proprietary envelope. The RFC says both impede interoperability, which is the objective of this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine getting a stamped receipt for your homework. If the receipt and the homework live in different drawers, they can get mixed up. This document gives them one shared folder.

sections.title: The TimeStampedData Structure
sections.content:
The new structure is built on the ContentInfo envelope of the Cryptographic Message Syntax (RFC 5652). CMS defines six content types; this memo adds a seventh, timestamped-data, identified by the object identifier id-ct-timestampedData (the last arc of its path is 31).

The content is a TimeStampedData sequence with these fields:

  • version: it SHALL be 1.
  • dataUri: a URI for retrieving the document. When content is absent, dataUri MUST be present.
  • metaData: optional details about the document, with a hashProtected flag plus optional fileName, mediaType and otherMetaData. At least one of those three sub-fields MUST be present.
  • content: the whole document in its original format and encoding. Leaving it out makes the evidence refer to external data, computed as though the content were present.
  • temporalEvidence: the proof that the document existed before a certain time.

The evidence is a CHOICE of an RFC 3161 token chain (tstEvidence), an Evidence Record from RFC 4998 (ersEvidence) or an otherEvidence with its own object identifier. Compliant applications are only required to support tstEvidence.
sections.plainLanguage: The folder has a label saying where the paper is, a cover note about it, the paper itself (or a note on where to find it), and the pile of date stamps.

sections.title: How the Token Chain Is Built
sections.content:
The tstEvidence choice holds a sequence with at least one TimeStampAndCRL element. Each element carries a TimeStampToken and, optionally, a CRL (Certificate Revocation List) from RFC 5280.

The rule for what each token covers is strict. The first token is computed over the value octets of content (or the octets fetched through dataUri). If metaData is present and hashProtected is TRUE, it is computed over the DER encoding of metaData followed by those content octets, so later changes to the metadata are detectable. The second token is computed over the first element, and every later token over the element before it.

The optional CRL shows that the certificate of the Time-Stamping Authority (TSA) that issued a token had not been revoked when the next element was added.
sections.plainLanguage: Each new stamp is put on top of the previous stamp, like stacking stamped sheets. The first sheet stamps the paper itself, and each later sheet stamps the one below it.

sections.title: Generating, Verifying and Extending
sections.content:
The RFC recommends processing steps for the RFC 3161 evidence type. To generate a structure, fill in version as 1, then either put the file in content (self-contained) or set dataUri (detached). Choose the hashProtected value if metadata is added, hash the covered data, obtain the first token from a TSA, wrap everything in a ContentInfo with the id-ct-timestampedData OID, and BER-encode it, except that otherMetaData attribute values MUST be DER encoded.

To verify, check the content type and version, check that the evidence is not empty, fetch the file through dataUri if needed, recompute the hash for the first token and compare it, then check that every token holds the right digest, was signed by a trusted TSA, and that the TSA certificate was not revoked when the next token was issued, based on the associated CRL.

To extend validity, validate the structure, store the latest available CRL in the last element, then obtain a new token over that last element and append it to the chain.
sections.plainLanguage: To make one, you stamp the paper and put it in the folder. To check one, you redo the stamping math and see that it matches. To keep it fresh, you add one more stamp on top.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Hash-protecting the metadata detects later alteration, but it does not prove the metadata was correct when the object was created. That has to be inferred some other way. For instance, it may be reasonable to trust metadata created by an archival service provider, but not metadata in an object received from an unknown party.

A time-stamp token should not generally be considered valid after the TSA certificate expires. A token can itself be time-stamped, and by repeating this a chain can extend the validity of the first token "ad libitum". Each additional token must be added in a timely manner, before the previous one expires or is revoked. This needs the TSA certificates to be verifiable long after expiry, typically with a CRL captured at the right time, since expired certificates are typically removed from CRLs regardless of revocation.
sections.plainLanguage: The stamps prove the paper has not changed since stamping, not that what the cover note says is true. And old stamps can fade, so you keep adding fresh ones before that happens.

data.title: TimeStampedData in ASN.1
data.code:
TimeStampedData ::= SEQUENCE {
   version              INTEGER { v1(1) },
   dataUri              IA5String OPTIONAL,
   metaData             MetaData OPTIONAL,
   content              OCTET STRING OPTIONAL,
   temporalEvidence     Evidence
}

viz.caption: WHAT EACH TIME-STAMP TOKEN IS COMPUTED OVER

cells: Value octets of content, or the octets from dataUri
DER of metaData, then the content octets
